prompt.en: Which action would NOT reduce confusion while several stations are helping with priority traffic?

text.en: Use plain language for names, places, and requested help.
Read back critical details before relaying them onward.
Keep routine comments off the channel until the priority traffic is handled.
Replace ordinary words with unexplained abbreviations so the exchange sounds more official.

explanation.en: Priority traffic needs accuracy more than style. Plain language, read-backs, and quiet routine stations reduce confusion; unexplained abbreviations add risk.

prompt.en: Which preparation would NOT help maintain communication with a handheld radio during an extended outage?

text.en: Charge spare battery packs before storm season.
Label a known-good charging cable and keep it with the radio.
Practice changing batteries without losing the current channel setting.
Store the only spare battery empty so it is fresh when the emergency starts.

explanation.en: A dead spare is not a reserve. Readiness depends on usable stored energy and a simple way to keep the handheld operating.

prompt.en: During a distress relay, an operator says, “I will write the location after the contact from memory.” What is the error?

text.en: Critical details should be written as they are received, then read back or relayed carefully.
Distress traffic should never include locations over amateur radio.
The operator should leave the frequency immediately after hearing the first distress word.
Only the signal report matters once a distress station is acknowledged.

explanation.en: Emergency communication is vulnerable to memory errors. Times, locations, call signs, and needed assistance should be captured accurately while the exchange is happening.
